title: Two Kinds of Leader in a Group
text:
Around 1950 the Harvard sociologist Robert Freed Bales built a room where small groups of students met to discuss and solve problems while trained observers watched through a one-way mirror. He developed a system for classifying every act in a conversation into categories such as giving suggestions, giving opinions, asking for information, agreeing, joking, showing tension or disagreeing.

Coding thousands of interactions, Bales saw that groups had to handle two kinds of demand at once. One was the task itself: proposing ideas, organizing and pushing toward a decision. The other was social and emotional: easing tension, encouraging others and holding the group together after disagreements.

In later analyses with Philip Slater, Bales found that these two roles were often filled by different people. Members tended to name one person as having the best ideas and doing the most to guide the discussion, and often a different person as the one they liked best. The task leader's push tended to create friction, and a well-liked member helped repair it. Groups seemed to work best when both functions were covered.
lesson: A team needs someone driving the work and someone holding people together. If you are the driver, value and support the person who mends relationships.
people: Robert Freed Bales; Philip Slater (later work)
source: Bales, R. F. (1950). Interaction Process Analysis: A Method for the Study of Small Groups. Addison-Wesley.
caveat: The clear split between the two roles was found mostly in groups of strangers; in established teams one person sometimes does both.
